slides.title: Concentrating Effort Where It Matters Most
bullets: A strategic imperative is a priority significant enough to concentrate resources on
The organization spends disproportionate time and attention on it
Rather than spreading effort evenly across every possible activity
It prevents the most common planning error: doing everything a little

slides.title: Imperatives Emerge from Situation Analysis
bullets: What is the biggest scientific risk or opportunity for this cycle
Which evidence gap, if closed, would most improve appropriate adoption
What competitive or regulatory shift demands a priority medical response
What unmet clinical or patient need represents the greatest opportunity

slides.title: Specific, Measurable, Patient-Connected
bullets: Specific, not generic: name the exact gap, population, and evidence
Example: closing a renal impairment evidence gap flagged in 80% of nephrologist interactions
Measurable, with a clear criterion for what progress looks like
Connected to a real patient or clinical benefit, not just an internal target

slides.title: Prioritizing Means Saying No
bullets: Deliberately giving up interesting activities outside the top priorities
This is uncomfortable, especially for motivated field teams
A plan that tries to prioritize everything ends up prioritizing nothing

slides.title: Imperatives Are Reviewed, Not Fixed
bullets: Reassessed at the annual planning cycle and whenever the environment shifts
Triggers include new competitive data, regulatory change, or a safety finding
A rigid plan that can't adapt its imperatives quickly loses its strategic value

slides.title: Imperatives Guide Daily Field Decisions
bullets: Knowing the current imperatives enables autonomous, coherent field decisions
Which congress to prioritize, which insight to escalate with urgency
Which relationship to invest in more heavily, without checking every call upward

takeaway.title: Strategic imperatives focus a Medical Plan's limited resources on what matters most
bullets: They emerge from situation analysis, not from intuition or habit
A strong imperative is specific, measurable, and tied to patient benefit
They are revisited whenever the competitive or regulatory picture changes
